sections.html:
Storm Damage Repair for Commercial Roofs in Winston-Salem

The Piedmont gets hit by two very different storm mechanisms in the same calendar year, and they damage roofs in different ways. Fast, high-wind summer thunderstorms can lift edge metal, tear membrane at fastening points, and drop hail on metal or single-ply roofs. Hurricane remnants tracking inland later in the season bring less wind but much more sustained rain, which finds every weak drain and marginal flashing detail a roof has. Our storm repair process assesses for both damage types rather than assuming one and missing the other.

Assessing Wind Damage

Wind damage on a low-slope commercial roof often starts at the edges, coping and edge metal are the first things a sustained gust gets under, and once edge metal lifts, the membrane behind it is exposed to further peeling. We check every parapet and roof edge after a wind event, along with rooftop equipment for shifted or loosened curb flashing, before assessing the field of the roof itself. On metal roof systems, which cover a fair number of the manufacturing buildings in this market including facilities around Tobaccoville and the industrial corridors near Kernersville, we check panel seams and fastener pull-through, since metal roofing fails differently than membrane systems under wind load.

Assessing Hail Damage

Hail impacts on single-ply membrane can bruise the material without an obvious puncture, which means damage isn't always visible on a surface walk. We check for granule loss on modified bitumen and cap sheet systems, and we inspect rooftop equipment housings and metal flashing for dents, which are often a more reliable indicator of hail size and impact force than the membrane itself. On metal roofing, hail denting is usually visible directly on the panels.

  • Edge metal and coping checked for lift or separation at every parapet
  • Membrane field inspected for wind-driven tears near fastening rows
  • Hail impact assessed via granule loss, membrane bruising, and metal denting
  • Rooftop equipment curbs and flashing checked for wind or impact damage
  • Drainage system checked for debris blockage from storm-driven material
  • All findings photographed and logged with date and estimated storm correlation

Hurricane Remnant Rainfall and Drainage Failure

By the time a tropical system reaches Forsyth County it's typically a tropical depression or post-tropical remnant, but the rainfall totals can still be significant and sustained over many hours. Roofs with adequate drain capacity handle this without issue; roofs with even minor existing drainage problems, a partially clogged scupper, a low spot with a couple inches of standing water under normal conditions, can see that water back up and find its way past flashing that would hold under lighter rain. Our post-storm inspection checks drainage function specifically, in addition to membrane condition, because rain-driven damage often traces back to a drainage issue rather than membrane failure.

Repair to Manufacturer Specification

Storm repair work follows the same manufacturer-spec requirement as any other repair on a roof under warranty, matching membrane type, using approved fastening patterns, and in some cases coordinating with the manufacturer's approved contractor process if the warranty requires it. We don't cut corners on storm repairs just because the timeline feels urgent; a repair that voids a warranty to save a day of scheduling costs the owner far more later.

Documentation for the Claims Process

Storm damage repair documentation is built with the insurance claims process in mind from the first site visit: dated photos correlated to the storm event, a written damage assessment separating pre-existing wear from new storm damage, and itemized repair scope. We provide this record to the owner or their adjuster as factual documentation, what we found and what we repaired, without making representations about claim approval, which is the carrier's determination based on the policy.

Repair Scheduling After Widespread Storm Events

After a storm that affects multiple properties across the region, we prioritize active leaks and life-safety concerns first, then work through the remaining queue by severity. We give property managers a realistic timeline based on actual workload rather than promising immediate response to every site simultaneously.

Repairing Metal Roof Systems After Storm Impact

Metal roofing common on manufacturing and distribution buildings in this market fails differently than membrane roofing under storm load. Panel seams can separate under wind uplift even when the panels themselves are undamaged, fasteners can back out or shear under repeated flex, and hail denting, while usually cosmetic, can concentrate stress at panel ribs over time if left unaddressed. We inspect fastener condition and seam integrity across the full panel run, extending beyond the visibly damaged section, since a storm event significant enough to damage one area typically stressed the whole roof plane.

Storm Damage Repair Questions

How do you tell storm damage apart from ordinary wear?

We document condition at every inspection and compare new findings against prior records where available, and we correlate damage patterns, wind-direction-consistent edge lift, hail-pattern denting, to the specific storm event date.

Does hail damage always show up as visible punctures?

No. Hail can bruise single-ply membrane without puncturing it, so we also check granule loss, metal flashing dents, and rooftop equipment housings, which often show impact more clearly than the membrane surface.

Why does a hurricane remnant with lower wind speeds still damage roofs?

The sustained heavy rainfall from a weakening tropical system can overwhelm marginal drainage that lighter rain wouldn't affect, so damage from these events is often drainage-related rather than wind-related.

Will storm repair work be done to manufacturer specification?

Yes, storm repairs follow the same manufacturer-spec and warranty-preservation process as any other repair work, including manufacturer-approved contractor requirements where the warranty calls for it.

What records do I get for an insurance claim?

Dated photos tied to the storm event, a written assessment distinguishing new damage from pre-existing wear, and an itemized repair scope, provided as factual documentation for the claims process.

sections.html:
Hail Damage Roof Insurance Claims in Winston-Salem

The Piedmont's spring and summer thunderstorm season brings hail to Winston-Salem most years, and commercial roofs take that damage very differently than the shingled residential roofs most hail coverage guidance is written around. A low-slope membrane doesn't shatter or lose granules the way asphalt shingles do, it bruises, and that bruising can sit invisible for months before it turns into a leak. Getting a hail-damaged commercial roof properly documented for a claim means understanding how each roofing system on a Winston-Salem building actually shows impact damage, not applying a residential inspection checklist to a flat roof.

How Hail Damages Low-Slope Commercial Membranes

On TPO, PVC, and EPDM membranes, hail impact typically shows as a soft, slightly depressed area where the membrane has been compressed against the insulation below, sometimes with a faint circular bruise pattern. It's rarely a hole at first, the damage is structural weakening of the membrane at that point, which becomes a leak path over subsequent freeze-thaw cycles or foot traffic. On built-up and modified bitumen roofs, common on Winston-Salem's older commercial and Innovation Quarter buildings, hail impact can fracture the surfacing layer or dislodge aggregate ballast, which is easy to miss without walking the full roof deck section by section.

What Hail Looks Like on Standing Seam and R-Panel Metal

Metal roofing is common on the distribution and industrial buildings along the I-40 and US-52 corridors, and hail damage there is more visually obvious but not always simple to evaluate. Denting on standing seam or R-panel systems can be purely cosmetic, or it can be significant enough to affect the panel's finish coating and long-term corrosion resistance, or in more severe impacts, compromise seams and fastener points where water intrusion actually starts. We document dent size, density per panel, and location relative to seams and penetrations, since that level of detail is what distinguishes a cosmetic issue from a functional one.

The Documentation Adjusters Look For After Hail

A hail claim moves faster when the documentation includes a roof plan marking every impact location, close-up photos at representative damage points, and, for membrane roofs, test cuts or probing where impact severity is in question. We also note hail size and direction where it's identifiable from impact patterns, correlated to any known storm activity for the area, which helps establish that the damage traces to a specific weather event rather than gradual wear.

Distinguishing Hail Bruising from Age-Related Wear

This is where hail claims most often get contested. A membrane with existing granule loss, seam fatigue, or general surface weathering can look similar to impact damage on a quick pass, and carriers scrutinize this distinction closely. We document both conditions side by side and honestly, new impact damage and any pre-existing wear, because a documentation package that blurs the line undermines its own credibility with whoever reviews it, adjuster or owner.

Hail on Coated and Recovered Roofs

A membrane that's already been treated with an acrylic or silicone coating, or a roof that's had an overlay recover, shows hail impact differently again, the coating layer can crack or delaminate at the impact point even when the membrane beneath is largely intact, which is a distinct failure mode from bare membrane bruising. On built-up roofs with a gravel or mineral cap sheet, hail can dislodge aggregate ballast in a scatter pattern that's easy to mistake for routine wear if the roof hasn't been walked section by section since the storm.

Filing Timeline After a Hail Event

Most commercial hail claims have a filing window that starts running from the date of loss, so documenting the roof promptly after a hailstorm, even before deciding whether the damage is significant enough to file, preserves the option. We're your roofing contractor, not a public adjuster: we inspect, document, and produce a repair scope for the adjuster to evaluate, and we don't file the claim, negotiate with the carrier, or guarantee an outcome.

Insurance Claim Questions

How do I know if my low-slope roof has hail damage?

Hail bruising on membrane roofs isn't always visible from the ground or even from a casual roof walk, it often shows as soft spots or granule displacement that only shows up under close inspection. If there's been a hail event and the roof hasn't been checked, an inspection before the next rain is worth scheduling.

Does hail dent on a metal roof always mean a claim is worth filing?

Cosmetic denting that doesn't affect the panel's water-shedding function is a different situation from denting that's compromised seams or fasteners. We document the extent and let the owner and adjuster evaluate it against the policy.

Can you tell hail damage apart from age-related wear on an older membrane?

Yes, impact damage has a distinct pattern (localized bruising or fracturing at the impact point) that reads differently under inspection than generalized granule loss or seam wear from age. We document both conditions honestly rather than attributing one to the other.

How soon after a hailstorm should the roof get inspected?

As soon as reasonably possible, and before any cleanup or unrelated repair work happens on the roof. Photographing hail damage in its original condition is what makes the documentation useful for a claim.

Will you meet with the insurance adjuster to review the hail damage?

Yes, we're available to walk the roof with an adjuster and point directly to documented impact locations, which is typically more useful than a report reviewed off site.

sections.html:
Wind and Storm Damage Roof Insurance Claims in Winston-Salem

Winston-Salem commercial roofs face two distinct wind events in a typical year, and they damage roofs in different ways. Spring and summer bring fast-moving severe thunderstorms with short bursts of straight-line wind that hit hard and move on, often leaving damage concentrated at a roof's weak points, loose flashing, an aging parapet cap, a section where fasteners had already started backing out. Later in the season, the remnants of tropical systems that track inland from the Gulf or Atlantic coast bring a different pattern: sustained wind over many hours combined with heavy, prolonged rainfall, which stresses the entire roof system rather than just its weak points and raises the odds of wind-driven water intrusion even where the membrane itself holds.

Where Wind Damage Starts on a Commercial Roof

Wind damage on a low-slope roof almost always starts at an edge, parapet coping, edge metal, or a mechanical curb, because that's where wind uplift generates the most force. Once a section of edge metal or coping lifts, wind gets underneath the adjacent membrane and the damage spreads from that starting point outward. We check these transition areas first on any post-storm inspection, since they're where uplift damage originates even when the field of the roof looks intact.

Wind-Driven Rain and Secondary Water Damage

A storm doesn't need to tear the membrane to cause a claimable loss. Sustained wind-driven rain can push water past flashing details that shed normal rainfall fine, and that water tracks into the building at points that aren't always visible from the roof surface. We document interior water staining alongside roof-level findings and correlate the two where the connection is clear, since insurance documentation for wind claims often needs both halves of that picture.

Documenting Uplift for a Wind Claim

Wind claims benefit from documentation that shows the direction and mechanism of the damage, which edge lifted first, where fasteners pulled through, whether membrane seams separated under uplift pressure or tore from debris impact. We photograph the failure points in sequence, note wind direction where it's evident from the damage pattern, and correlate the event to any known storm activity for the date in question.

Debris Impact on Top of Wind Uplift

Winston-Salem's tree canopy means a wind event often brings debris impact along with straight uplift force, a limb or larger branch coming down on a membrane roof punctures or tears it directly, which is a different damage mechanism from wind lifting an edge on its own, even though both can happen in the same storm. We document the two separately, since a puncture from debris and a seam failure from uplift call for different repair details even when they show up on the same claim.

Emergency Mitigation Before the Adjuster Arrives

When a wind event leaves an active leak, protecting the building comes first, we provide emergency tarp and dry-in to stop ongoing water intrusion, documenting the original damage with photos before any tarping covers it. Carriers generally expect reasonable mitigation to prevent further loss, and having that documented protects the claim rather than complicating it.

What This Documentation Is, and Isn't

We're your roofing contractor, not a public adjuster, our role is inspecting the roof, documenting wind damage with photos and a written assessment, and producing a repair scope that reflects the full extent of what happened. We don't negotiate with the carrier, characterize what a settlement should be, or guarantee claim approval; that determination sits with the adjuster working against the specific policy.

Working From the Same Documentation Twice

Property owners occasionally need the same wind-damage documentation more than once, first for the insurance claim itself, then again for a lender or property-management review, or for a warranty inquiry with the roofing manufacturer if the damaged section was under an active system warranty. We keep the documentation format consistent across those uses so the same photos, measurements, and written assessment can support each one without a separate inspection every time.

Insurance Claim Questions

Does a fallen tree limb count as wind damage for a claim?

Typically yes, since the tree came down because of wind, we document the impact, the resulting roof damage, and photograph the debris before it's cleared, which supports that connection for the claim.

What's the difference between wind damage from a thunderstorm and from a hurricane remnant?

Thunderstorm winds tend to be short, intense bursts that cause localized damage at a roof's weak points, while tropical remnants bring sustained wind over hours combined with heavy rain, which stresses the whole roof system and increases the chance of wind-driven water intrusion even where the membrane itself holds.

Should I tarp a wind-damaged roof before the adjuster sees it?

Emergency mitigation to stop ongoing water intrusion is standard and usually expected by carriers, but we photograph and document the damage first, before any tarping, so the original condition is on record.

Can wind damage be present without visible membrane tears?

Yes, wind can loosen fasteners or partially lift a membrane at the edge or seams without an obvious tear, which can go unnoticed until the next storm makes it worse. That's part of why a post-storm inspection matters even when nothing looks obviously wrong from the ground.

Do you handle emergency tarping if wind damage needs immediate mitigation?

Yes, we provide emergency tarp and dry-in service alongside the documentation, so the building is protected from further water intrusion while the claim moves forward.

sections.html:
Commercial Roof Insurance Claim Assistance in Winston-Salem

A commercial roof claim in Winston-Salem usually starts the same way, a tenant reports a ceiling stain after a storm, a property manager notices ponding water on a walk-through, or a routine inspection turns up wind-lifted membrane at a parapet edge. What happens in the days right after matters more than most owners expect: whether the damage gets photographed before cleanup crews change what's visible, whether the full repair scope makes it into the adjuster's file, and whether the finished repair actually meets current code. We work this process as the roofing contractor, inspecting, documenting, and producing a scope an adjuster can evaluate, not as a public adjuster or claims negotiator.

What a Roof Claim Actually Requires

Winston-Salem's commercial roof stock is not uniform, and that shapes what a claim needs. Downtown, the tobacco-era brick warehouses converted through Innovation Quarter often carry built-up or modified bitumen roofs installed in layers over decades, where hail or wind damage can be harder to separate from ordinary aging without a close inspection. Newer buildings tied to the Wake Forest medical and research corridor tend to run single-ply TPO, which shows wind and hail damage differently, seam stress and membrane punctures rather than layer separation. Distribution buildings along the I-40 and US-52 corridors are frequently metal R-panel, where hail shows up as denting and wind shows up at the panel seams and fasteners. Each roof type calls for its own documentation approach, matched to how that system actually fails.

Documenting Damage Before the Adjuster Arrives

The strongest claims start with documentation captured before repair or cleanup work changes the roof. That means a roof plan marking every damage location, photographs at each spot, and, where the membrane allows it, moisture readings to check whether water has already tracked into the insulation layer. We record what type of damage we're looking at and note it separately from any pre-existing wear the roof already had, since conflating the two is one of the more common reasons a claim gets contested later.

Meeting the Adjuster on the Roof

We're available to walk the roof directly with an insurance adjuster or a property owner's public adjuster and point to specific findings on site. That tends to move faster than a written report reviewed off site, since the adjuster can ask about a specific seam, panel, or drain in real time and get a direct answer about what caused it and what repairing it correctly involves.

Framing a Complete Repair Scope

A scope that only covers the visibly damaged section often undercounts what code actually requires. If a membrane section is being replaced, current code may call for updated insulation R-values or edge-metal detailing that didn't exist when the roof was originally installed, and a repair that ignores that gets flagged during permitting even if the insurance settlement didn't account for it. We itemize the scope by roof section, referencing manufacturer specifications for materials, so the adjuster is working from a cost basis that reflects what a compliant repair actually takes, not a lump-sum estimate that's hard to verify against the damage.

When a Claim Comes Back Denied or Underpaid

If a settlement looks short relative to the documented damage, we can re-inspect and check whether areas were missed or whether the scope undercounted repair requirements like code-mandated upgrades. That additional documentation goes to the owner to use with the carrier or their own adjuster, we don't dispute the carrier's determination directly or represent the owner in that conversation, since that's outside what a roofing contractor is positioned to do.

What We Don't Do

We're your roofing contractor, not a public adjuster, we document and substantiate the roof damage so you and your adjuster work from an accurate scope, rather than filing the claim, negotiating on the owner's behalf, or guaranteeing what a carrier will approve. Every finding in our documentation reflects what we actually observed on the roof, whether that helps or complicates a given claim.

Insurance Claim Questions

Does insurance cover a full commercial roof replacement?

It depends on the policy, the cause of loss, and whether the damage is repairable to specification or requires full replacement. We document the actual condition and provide a scope; the carrier makes the coverage determination against the policy language.

What does the roofing contractor actually do in a claim, versus a public adjuster?

We inspect the roof, document damage with photos and measurements, and produce a repair scope the adjuster can evaluate. We don't file the claim, negotiate the settlement, or represent the owner to the carrier, that's the distinction between a roofing contractor and a public adjuster.

What happens if my claim comes back denied or the payout looks short?

We can re-inspect and check whether the documentation covered the full damage extent, including any areas that may have been missed on the first pass. We provide that additional record to the owner to use however they choose with the carrier.

Who decides whether a section gets repaired or replaced?

The adjuster makes that call based on the documented damage and the policy, but the repair-versus-replace line usually follows the manufacturer's own repairability guidance for that membrane and how much of the roof section is affected.

How fast can you get out to document damage after a storm?

We prioritize storm-damage documentation requests, since photographing damage before any cleanup or repair work happens is what makes it usable for a claim. Call as soon as damage is noticed, even before deciding whether to file.

sections.html:
Insurance Documentation Support for Winston-Salem Commercial Roofs

When a commercial roof has storm or leak damage that's headed toward an insurance claim, the documentation an adjuster receives shapes how smoothly that claim moves. Our role is to produce a factual, organized record of roof condition and damage, photos, measurements, and a written assessment, that gives the owner and the adjuster the same accurate starting point. We don't represent the insurance carrier and we don't predict what a carrier will approve; that determination belongs to the adjuster working against the specific policy.

What Goes Into a Documentation Package

A documentation package starts with a roof plan showing damage locations, followed by photographs at each location taken before any repair or cleanup work changes what's visible. We note damage type, wind lift, hail impact, water intrusion path, and separate that from any pre-existing wear the roof already showed, since conflating storm damage with ordinary age-related deterioration is one of the more common reasons a claim gets disputed. Where the damage relates to a specific storm event, we note the date and correlate it to known weather data for the area where relevant.

  • Roof plan marked with all damage locations
  • Photographs at each location, taken before repair or cleanup
  • Damage type documented and distinguished from pre-existing wear
  • Storm event date noted and correlated to the damage where applicable
  • Itemized repair scope with materials and labor broken out by roof section
  • Manufacturer specification references included for proposed repair materials

Working Alongside Adjusters and Public Adjusters

We're available to walk a roof with an insurance adjuster or a property owner's public adjuster and point to specific findings directly on site, this is often more useful than a report alone, since it lets the adjuster ask questions about a specific detail in real time. We answer factually about what we observed and what repair method the damage calls for; we don't advocate for a claim outcome or characterize what the carrier should pay, since that's outside what a roofing contractor is positioned to determine.

Documentation for Ongoing Maintenance History

Carriers increasingly ask for proof of ongoing roof maintenance as part of a claim review, particularly where a policy has a maintenance-related exclusion. Owners enrolled in our preventive maintenance program already have a dated visit history that supports this kind of request. For owners without that history, we can document current condition as a baseline, though we're clear that a single inspection doesn't substitute for an ongoing maintenance record if a carrier is specifically asking for that.

Distinguishing Storm Damage From Pre-Existing Condition

This is often the most contested part of a commercial roof claim, and it's where clear documentation matters most. A membrane that already had granule loss or seam wear before a hail event looks different under close inspection than fresh impact damage, and we document both conditions honestly rather than attributing pre-existing wear to the storm to strengthen a claim. This protects the credibility of the whole documentation package, which matters more for the owner's long-term standing with the carrier than winning one contested line item.

Repair Scope Documentation for Claim Settlement

Once damage is documented, we provide an itemized repair scope broken out by roof section, referencing the manufacturer system and materials required to repair to specification. This gives the adjuster a concrete cost basis to evaluate against the policy rather than a lump-sum estimate that's harder to verify line by line.

What We Don't Do

We don't inflate damage scope, don't claim outcomes we can't guarantee, and don't represent that we can get a claim approved, any framing along those lines misrepresents both the claims process and our role in it. Our documentation is built to be defensible under scrutiny from any party reviewing it, because that's what actually serves the owner's interest through a claims process that can stretch over months.

Documentation Timing Relative to the Claim Filing

Where possible, we prefer to document damage before the owner files the claim, since that gives the initial filing accurate supporting material from the start rather than requiring a follow-up submission later. When we're brought in after a claim is already filed, we document current condition and note where our findings align with or differ from any prior assessment already on file, without disputing another party's report directly, our documentation stands on its own as an independent record of what we observed on the date of our visit.

Insurance Documentation Questions

Can you tell me whether my insurance will approve a roof claim?

No, claim approval is the carrier's determination based on the policy terms. We provide factual damage documentation and repair scope; we don't predict or guarantee claim outcomes.

Will you meet with my insurance adjuster on site?

Yes, we're available to walk the roof with an adjuster or public adjuster and point to documented findings directly, which is often clearer than a written report reviewed off site.

How do you separate storm damage from normal wear in the documentation?

We assess membrane condition characteristics specific to each damage type, impact patterns for hail, tear direction for wind, and document pre-existing wear honestly alongside new damage rather than attributing one to the other.

Does a maintenance history help with a claim?

It can, since some carriers request proof of ongoing maintenance, particularly where a policy has a maintenance-related exclusion. A dated visit history from an ongoing maintenance program supports that kind of request more directly than a single inspection.

What format is the repair scope provided in for claim review?

An itemized breakdown by roof section, referencing manufacturer specification for proposed materials, giving the adjuster a verifiable cost basis rather than a single lump sum.

sections.html:
Snow and Ice Roof Damage Insurance Claims in Winston-Salem

Winston-Salem's winter roof risk looks different from what the term "snow damage" usually brings to mind. The Piedmont sits in a spot where cold air damming against the Blue Ridge to the west can trap a shallow layer of freezing air near the ground while milder air moves in above it, and the result is often freezing rain rather than deep snow. For a commercial roof, an ice event like that creates its own set of problems, weight on parapets and rooftop equipment, blocked drains, and water that backs up during the thaw, that a claim needs to be documented around specifically, not treated as generic snow-load damage.

Why the Piedmont Gets Ice Instead of Snow

Because the freezing layer during a Piedmont ice event is often shallow and sits right at the surface, precipitation frequently falls as rain and freezes on contact rather than accumulating as snow. That means ice tends to coat every horizontal and near-horizontal surface on a roof evenly, the membrane field, parapet caps, drain bowls, equipment housings, rather than piling up in drifts the way snow does. The practical effect for a claim is that ice-related roof damage is often about accumulated weight and blocked drainage across the whole roof rather than a load concentration in one area.

Ice Load on Rooftop Equipment and Parapets

Rooftop HVAC units, condensate lines, and older parapet coping are common points of ice-related failure. Ice buildup can crack condensate lines or unit housings that then leak once temperatures rise, and repeated freeze-thaw cycling can work parapet coping or flashing loose at joints that were already marginal. We inspect these specific points after an ice event, since damage there is easy to miss from ground level or a quick roof walk.

Drain and Scupper Backups From Ice

Roof drains and scuppers are especially vulnerable during an ice event, a drain bowl or scupper opening that ices over stops functioning entirely, and any additional rain or meltwater has nowhere to go until it thaws. That standing water adds weight the roof structure wasn't necessarily designed to hold for an extended period, and it can back up under flashing at penetrations and parapets, causing interior leaks that don't show up until well after the storm has passed.

Older Built-Up Roofs and Repeated Freeze-Thaw

Downtown Winston-Salem's older tobacco-era buildings often carry built-up roofing that's been recovered or patched over multiple decades, and those layered systems respond to repeated freeze-thaw cycling differently than a newer single-ply membrane. Trapped moisture between layers can freeze, expand, and work a seam or lap loose over the course of one ice event, then do it again in the next one, which is why an ice-related claim on an older built-up roof sometimes traces back to a weak point that had been quietly developing over several winters rather than a single storm.

Documenting Ice-Related Roof Damage

Ice damage documentation has a timing challenge that hail and wind claims don't: some of the evidence disappears when the ice melts. We document conditions as soon as it's safe to access the roof, then follow up after thaw to check drains, flashing, and equipment for damage that only becomes apparent once the ice is gone, cracked lines, displaced coping, or interior staining from a backup that occurred during the event.

Timing Claims Around a Multi-Day Ice Event

A Piedmont ice event can span several days between the initial freeze and full thaw, and documentation often needs two visits to capture the full picture, one during or immediately after the event, and a follow-up once conditions clear. We're your roofing contractor, not a public adjuster: we inspect, document, and produce a repair scope reflecting what we found at each stage, and we don't file the claim or negotiate with the carrier on the owner's behalf.

Insurance Claim Questions

Does the Piedmont get enough snow to cause commercial roof claims?

Snow load itself is rarely the issue here, the more common problem is freezing rain and ice accumulation, which coats a roof and adds weight and drainage blockage without the depth people associate with snow load damage further north.

Why does Winston-Salem get ice storms instead of straight snow?

Cold air damming against the Blue Ridge to the west can trap a shallow layer of freezing air at the surface while warmer air moves in above it, and precipitation falls as rain that freezes on contact, a pattern that produces ice accumulation more often than it produces deep snow in the Piedmont.

Can ice damage rooftop HVAC units?

Yes, ice accumulation on curbs, condensate lines, and unit housings can crack components or block drainage that then backs water up into the roof assembly once conditions thaw. We check rooftop equipment specifically during a post-ice-storm inspection.

What does an ice-related roof claim typically document?

Photos of ice accumulation and its effects where still visible, drain and scupper condition once ice clears, any parapet or coping displacement from ice weight, and interior water staining from backed-up drainage during the thaw.

How long after an ice storm should the roof be checked?

As soon as it's safe to access the roof, some damage, like a cracked drain line or displaced flashing, isn't visible until the ice has fully melted, so a follow-up inspection after thaw is often as important as the initial one.

items.name: Commercial Reroofing in Winston-Salem, NC
items.meta: Full commercial reroofing for Winston-Salem property owners: tear-off or recover, code-compliant assemblies, manufacturer-backed warranties, and a documented specification package.

sections.html:
Reroofing Projects for Winston-Salem Commercial Properties

A reroof is a procurement decision as much as a construction project. We scope Winston-Salem reroofs against the applicable building code section, the manufacturer's current specification, and the owner's budget cycle, then put the whole thing in writing before a crew touches the building. Whether the asset is a Hanesbrands-adjacent distribution shed, a medical office building near Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist, or a mid-2000s office park roof off Piedmont Triad Research Park, the process is the same: assess, specify, document, execute.

Tear-Off vs. Recover: How We Make the Call

North Carolina's building code follows the International Building Code with state amendments, and that code sets the threshold for how many roof layers can remain before a full tear-off is mandatory. We pull the roof's permit history where available and core the membrane in two or three locations to confirm layer count, insulation condition, and deck moisture. If the substrate is dry and within layer limits, a recover assembly over the existing membrane can meet code and cut project cost. If we find wet insulation, deteriorated fasteners, or a deck that won't hold a mechanically attached system, we specify tear-off.

We never default to tear-off because it's the safer sell. A recover done to spec, with the right cover board and fastening pattern for the wind zone, performs as well as new construction on a properly maintained deck. The decision goes in the proposal with the moisture-scan data attached, not as a verbal assurance.

Specification and Manufacturer Compliance

Every reroof we bid references a specific manufacturer system, Carlisle SynTec, GAF, Holcim Elevate, Johns Manville, Sika Sarnafil, or Versico depending on what the building and budget call for. The spec sheet lists membrane thickness, attachment method, fastener spacing per the wind uplift calculation for Forsyth County, insulation R-value, and cover board type. This matters for two reasons: it's what lets us pull a manufacturer-backed warranty instead of a workmanship-only warranty, and it's what a facilities director or property manager needs on file for insurance and lender requirements.

  • Deck and insulation moisture survey with core samples logged by location
  • Wind uplift calculation specific to the building's height and exposure category
  • Manufacturer system selection matched to substrate and expected roof traffic
  • Fastening pattern and cover board spec documented in the proposal
  • Permit pull and inspection scheduling coordinated with the local jurisdiction
  • Warranty registration paperwork submitted at project close

Working Around Occupied and Institutional Buildings

A large share of the reroof work in this market sits on buildings that can't just shut down, hospital-adjacent medical offices, manufacturing lines running shifts, multifamily buildings with residents on site. We stage material delivery, crane placement, and daily tear-back limits around what the building's operation can tolerate. On the Innovation Quarter side of downtown, that often means coordinating loading dock access and noise windows with building management in advance. On a Kernersville or Union Cross distribution building, it means keeping dock doors clear and confirming which bays stay operational during the reroof.

Daily tear-back is limited to what we can dry in before end of shift, no exceptions, regardless of forecast. A crew leaves the building sealed every night it's occupied, full stop.

Warranty Structure and What It Actually Covers

Manufacturer warranties on a reroof come in tiers, material-only, system, and no-dollar-limit, and the tier available depends on whether the installing crew is factory-certified for that manufacturer and whether the full assembly, cover board and insulation included, matches the spec. We tell owners up front which tier their project qualifies for and what triggers a warranty denial: unapproved rooftop penetrations, third-party equipment installed without a manufacturer-reviewed detail, or maintenance neglect documented in an inspection. A workmanship warranty from us covers installation separately and runs concurrent with the manufacturer term.

Reroofing Costs and Procurement Timing

Because reroofing is a capital expense, most of the property managers and REIT-owned assets we work with need a proposal that fits a budget cycle, not a same-week decision. We provide a scope document with unit pricing broken out by roof section so a facilities team can present it internally, get board or ownership sign-off, and schedule the work for a maintenance window rather than an emergency. For manufacturing and healthcare-adjacent buildings, that often means targeting a shutdown period or lower-occupancy season.

Common Questions on Winston-Salem Reroofing Projects

How do you know if a roof needs tear-off instead of a recover?

We core the roof in multiple spots to check for wet insulation, count existing layers against code limits, and inspect deck condition. If the deck and insulation are sound and layer count is within code, recover is usually viable and documented in the proposal with the core data attached.

Will the reroof disrupt operations at an occupied building?

We plan daily work sections so the roof is fully dried in and watertight before crews leave each day, and we coordinate dock access, parking, and noise windows with building management in advance, particularly for medical office and manufacturing sites.

What warranty comes with a commercial reroof?

Manufacturer warranty tier depends on the system installed and certification status of the crew; we specify which tier the project qualifies for in the proposal, plus a separate workmanship warranty on the installation itself.

Do you handle the permit process?

Yes. We pull the required permit through the local jurisdiction and schedule inspections as part of the project timeline, and that documentation becomes part of the closeout package alongside warranty registration.

How is pricing structured for a large or multi-building reroof?

We break pricing out by roof section or building so a property management or ownership group can phase the work across budget cycles rather than committing to a single lump sum.

items.name: Roof Recover & Overlay in Winston-Salem, NC
items.meta: Roof recover and overlay assessment for Winston-Salem buildings, with layer-count review, moisture scan, and code-compliant assembly documentation before install.

sections.html:
Recover and Overlay Assessment for Winston-Salem Roofs

Recover means installing a new roof assembly over an existing one that's still structurally sound, rather than tearing the old system off first, and it's the option that saves an owner the most money when the underlying deck and insulation qualify. It's also the option most often oversold by contractors who skip the assessment step, which is why every recover proposal we write starts with data, not a visual estimate from the ground.

What Has to Be True for Recover to Be Viable

Three conditions have to hold before we'll propose a recover instead of tear-off: the deck has to test structurally sound, the existing insulation has to test dry through core samples, and the existing roof's layer count has to fall within what North Carolina's building code allows to remain in place before a new layer is added. Any one of these failing rules out recover regardless of how the roof looks from the parking lot.

We pull permit history where it's available to establish prior roof work, and where records don't exist or don't match what we find in the field, the core samples become the record of layer count instead.

Insulation Crush Testing

Beyond moisture, we check whether existing insulation can support a new membrane system without crushing or compressing under foot traffic and mechanically fastened attachment, which matters more on older or lower-density insulation board than owners typically expect. Compressed insulation reduces both R-value and the new membrane's fastener pull-out resistance, so this test result factors directly into whether we recommend recover or a tear-off with fresh insulation instead.

  • Existing layer count confirmed against North Carolina building code limits
  • Deck structural condition assessed for added dead load if applicable
  • Insulation moisture checked via core samples at multiple roof zones
  • Insulation crush resistance tested against new membrane attachment requirements
  • Cover board specified to separate new membrane from existing surface irregularities
  • Manufacturer warranty tier confirmed for the specific recover assembly

Code Limits on Roof Layers

Building code sets a maximum number of roof layers that can remain on a structure before a full tear-off is required regardless of substrate condition, which means a roof that's already been recovered once may already be at its limit. We confirm layer count before quoting recover as an option at all, since proposing a recover on a roof that's already at the code maximum isn't a cost-saving measure, it's a compliance problem waiting to surface at inspection or resale.

Financial Case for Recover vs. Full Replacement

Recover typically costs less than tear-off and replacement because it eliminates demolition labor, disposal cost, and the schedule risk of an exposed deck during installation, which matters especially on occupied buildings, manufacturing floors and medical offices among them, where minimizing downtime carries its own value beyond the roofing invoice itself. We lay out both options side by side in the proposal when a roof genuinely qualifies for either, so the owner is deciding with full cost and risk information rather than being steered toward whichever option is easier to sell.

Typical Recover Assembly Configurations

On low-slope membrane roofs, a common recover assembly places a new cover board over the existing membrane, mechanically fastened through to the deck rather than adhered to the old surface, followed by the new membrane attached to that cover board per the manufacturer's fastening spec. On metal roofs being recovered with a new low-slope membrane or a retrofit standing seam system, the assembly instead typically involves a retrofit framing or purlin system that creates a new mounting plane above the existing panels, since a membrane can't be reliably adhered to ribbed metal without that intermediate structure.

Which configuration applies depends entirely on what the existing roof is built from, and we specify the assembly type in the proposal rather than using a generic recover description that doesn't distinguish between a low-slope membrane recover and a metal roof retrofit.

Documentation for Warranty and Ownership Records

A recover project gets the same closeout documentation as a full tear-off: as-built assembly details, core sample and moisture survey data, manufacturer warranty registration, and permit and inspection records. This matters particularly for recover projects, since a future buyer, insurer, or facilities manager needs to know that a roof is a layered assembly and what's underneath the current surface.

Questions on Roof Recover and Overlay

How do you know if a roof qualifies for recover instead of tear-off?

We confirm the deck is structurally sound, insulation tests dry through core samples, and existing layer count is within code limits. All three have to hold for recover to be a viable, code-compliant option.

Is recover always cheaper than tear-off?

Usually, since it avoids demolition and disposal cost, but it's only appropriate when the underlying roof genuinely qualifies. We don't recommend recover just because it's the lower-cost option on paper.

What happens if a roof is already at the code layer limit?

Recover isn't an option at that point regardless of surface condition; a full tear-off is required to bring the roof into compliance before a new system can be installed.

Does insulation condition affect the recover decision?

Yes. Wet or crushed insulation can rule out recover even if the deck and layer count otherwise qualify, since it affects both R-value and the new membrane's attachment performance.

What documentation comes with a recover project?

The same closeout package as a full replacement: as-built details, core sample and moisture data, warranty registration, and permit and inspection records.

items.meta: TPO membrane systems for Winston-Salem medical and distribution roofs, specified by mil thickness, wind uplift rating, and manufacturer warranty tier.

sections.html:
TPO Membrane Systems for Winston-Salem Buildings

TPO is the single-ply membrane we specify most often on Winston-Salem low-slope roofs, and for a narrow set of reasons: heat-welded seams that test stronger than the membrane itself, a reflective white surface that helps offset summer cooling load, and a manufacturer field that includes Carlisle SynTec, GAF, Holcim Elevate, and Versico all producing current, well-documented systems. We specify it by mil thickness and attachment method, not as a generic membrane line item.

Why Reflectivity Matters on Medical and Lab Roofs

A white TPO surface reduces rooftop surface temperature compared to a black membrane, which matters directly on buildings running heavy mechanical cooling loads, a medical office building near the Atrium Health Wake Forest Baptist campus, or a lab buildout inside Innovation Quarter where converted tobacco-warehouse floor plates now hold sensitive equipment. Lower surface temperature also slows long-term membrane aging from UV and thermal cycling, which is a factor worth naming on a 20-year system rather than treating reflectivity as a marketing point.

Reflectivity isn't the only variable, though. On a building with heavy foot traffic for rooftop equipment service, we'll often add a walkway pad system to protect the membrane at access points regardless of color.

Mil Thickness and Attachment Method

We spec TPO most commonly in 60-mil or 80-mil thickness, with the heavier mil reserved for roofs with expected higher foot traffic, ballast exposure, or a longer intended service life before recover. Attachment runs one of three ways: mechanically fastened, fully adhered, or induction-welded, and the choice depends on deck type, wind exposure category, and whether the building's insurance carrier or lender has specified a minimum uplift rating.

Fastening pattern isn't a fixed number we carry from job to job. It's calculated against the building's height, corner and perimeter zone geometry, and Forsyth County's basic wind speed, then documented in the proposal alongside the mil thickness and attachment method.

  • Membrane thickness specified in mils, matched to expected traffic and service life
  • Attachment method selected for deck type and wind exposure category
  • Heat-welded seam testing performed during installation, not assumed from spec
  • Walkway pads specified at rooftop equipment access points
  • Flashing detail matched to manufacturer's current published standard
  • Warranty tier confirmed in writing before installation begins

Seam Welding and Quality Control

TPO's heat-welded seam is the system's strongest point when done correctly and its most common failure point when it isn't. Weld quality depends on machine temperature, ambient temperature, and roller pressure, all of which shift through a work day in Piedmont summer heat. We probe seams during installation rather than relying on a visual pass at the end, because a cold weld can look sealed and still fail under wind uplift or foot traffic within a few seasons.

Where TPO Fits on Distribution and Manufacturing Roofs

Large flat roofs on distribution buildings along the US-52 and I-40 corridors, including facilities near Hanesbrands' distribution operations, are common TPO candidates because of the membrane's ballasted and mechanically fastened options for wide-open decks with minimal rooftop clutter. On these buildings, cost per square foot and speed of installation over large areas usually favor TPO over PVC or fully adhered EPDM, unless there's a specific chemical exposure concern that points toward PVC instead.

Cool Roof Credit Under the Energy Code

North Carolina's energy code, based on the International Energy Conservation Code with state amendments, allows some reflective roof assemblies to factor into a building's overall energy compliance path, particularly on buildings pursuing a prescriptive path rather than a full envelope performance calculation. White TPO's reflectivity rating is documented data we can pull from the manufacturer's product listing when a design team needs it for an energy code submittal, rather than a number we estimate.

This matters most on new construction and full replacement scopes where the design team is assembling an energy code compliance package, and less on a straightforward recover where the existing building's compliance path was already established. We flag which category a given project falls into early, since it affects what documentation the design team needs from us.

Manufacturer Warranty Structure

TPO warranties run material-only, system, or no-dollar-limit depending on the manufacturer and whether the full assembly, membrane included, matches that manufacturer's current specification. We confirm which tier a given project qualifies for before signing, and we register the warranty as part of project closeout rather than leaving that step to the owner after the fact.

Common Questions on TPO Roofing Projects

How is TPO different from PVC?

Both are heat-welded single-ply membranes, but PVC generally offers stronger resistance to grease, oils, and certain chemical exposures, while TPO is typically lower cost per square foot for large open roof areas without that exposure concern.

What mil thickness should a building use?

We base mil thickness on expected foot traffic, ballast, and intended service life before a future recover, and specify it in writing rather than defaulting to a single standard thickness across every project.

Does color affect the roof's performance?

White TPO reduces rooftop surface temperature relative to darker membranes, which can reduce mechanical cooling load and slow UV-driven membrane aging over the system's service life.

How long does a TPO system typically last before recover is considered?

Service life depends on mil thickness, attachment method, and maintenance, and we discuss expected service life as part of the initial proposal rather than after installation.

What warranty comes with a TPO installation?

Warranty tier depends on the manufacturer and full assembly compliance; we name the tier in writing before the contract is signed and handle registration at project closeout.

sections.html:
Acrylic Coating for Metal and Well-Drained Winston-Salem Roofs

A coating recommendation starts with adhesion, moisture, drainage, membrane condition, detail preparation, and warranty eligibility, not every existing roof is a restoration candidate. Acrylic coating is the lower-cost restoration option we specify where a roof drains properly and doesn't carry a standing water condition, most often on standing seam and R-panel metal roofs approaching the point where recoating extends service life without a full replacement. It costs less than silicone per square foot but doesn't tolerate ponding the way silicone does, so drainage condition determines which coating we recommend more than any other single factor.

Why Drainage Determines the Coating Choice

We check roof slope and drainage patterns before proposing acrylic over silicone, because acrylic's lower cost only makes sense where the roof actually sheds water reliably. A metal roof with functioning ridge-to-eave drainage and no low spots holding water after a storm is a straightforward acrylic candidate; a flat roof with any documented ponding history gets steered toward silicone regardless of the cost difference, because the wrong coating choice fails faster than no coating at all.

This is a judgment call we make in writing, with the drainage assessment documented, rather than defaulting to whichever coating carries a lower line-item price on the proposal.

Reflectivity and Metal Roof Restoration

A large share of our acrylic coating work is on aging metal roofs, exposed-fastener R-panel and standing seam alike, where the factory finish has chalked or faded and reflectivity has dropped from its original specification. Acrylic coating restores reflective performance and adds a fresh weather barrier over sound metal, which can meaningfully extend service life on a roof that's structurally fine but cosmetically and reflectively past its useful coating life.

  • Roof slope and drainage confirmed to rule out ponding before acrylic is proposed
  • Substrate cleaned and prepped to manufacturer surface-preparation standard
  • Existing fastener and seam condition inspected and repaired before coating
  • Dry film thickness specified in mils and documented at application
  • Reflectivity rating confirmed against the manufacturer's published data
  • Recoat interval documented based on substrate and exposure

Surface Preparation Before Coating

Acrylic coating adhesion depends heavily on surface preparation, particularly on metal roofs where chalking, oxidation, or residual mill finish can prevent proper bond if the surface isn't cleaned and, in some cases, primed first. We treat surface prep as its own line item in the scope rather than an assumed step, since a coating applied over an improperly prepped surface will delaminate well before its expected service life regardless of coating quality.

Cost Comparison to Silicone

Acrylic typically costs less per square foot than silicone, both in material and in some cases application labor, which makes it the more economical choice on the roofs where it's appropriate. We're direct about that cost difference in every proposal, and equally direct about where acrylic isn't the right fit, since choosing the cheaper coating on a roof with a ponding condition costs an owner more in the long run through premature failure.

Elastomeric Flexibility in Cold Weather

Acrylic coatings stay flexible enough to bridge minor hairline cracks and fastener movement at typical service temperatures, but flexibility drops as temperature drops, and a hard freeze during application or shortly after can affect cure and early-life flexibility more than it would with silicone. We track forecast temperature closely when scheduling acrylic application in late fall or winter, and we won't apply coating ahead of a freeze event before it's had adequate cure time, regardless of a tight project schedule.

This is a seasonal scheduling constraint specific to acrylic that doesn't apply the same way to silicone, and it's one of the practical tradeoffs of the lower material cost that we walk owners through before they commit to a winter application window.

Recoat Scheduling and Documentation

Acrylic coatings have a defined recoat interval based on substrate, exposure, and applied thickness, and we document that interval in writing at project completion so an owner or facilities team has a maintenance date on the calendar rather than waiting for visible failure before scheduling the next coat. This kind of documentation is also what a property management firm typically needs on file for a capital planning budget.

Documenting the Recommendation for Ownership Review

Because acrylic and silicone are frequently compared side by side by an owner or facilities committee deciding on a restoration budget, we put the drainage assessment, substrate condition, and cost comparison between the two options in writing rather than delivering the recommendation verbally. That documentation is what lets a property management firm or ownership group defend the coating choice internally, and it becomes part of the record a future facilities manager can reference when the next recoat interval comes due.

Frequently Asked Questions on Acrylic Roof Coatings

When is acrylic the better choice over silicone?

When the roof drains properly with no documented ponding condition. Acrylic costs less but doesn't hold up to sustained standing water the way silicone does.

Does acrylic work on metal roofs?

Yes, it's one of the most common substrates we coat with acrylic, particularly on aging standing seam and R-panel roofs where the factory finish has chalked or faded.

How important is surface preparation before coating?

Very. Chalking, oxidation, or mill finish residue can prevent proper adhesion if the surface isn't cleaned and, in some cases, primed before coating.

How is coating thickness confirmed?

We specify a target dry film thickness in mils and document what's actually applied, since reflectivity and service life both depend on that number.

How often does an acrylic-coated roof need to be recoated?

Interval depends on substrate and exposure, and we document a specific recoat date at project completion rather than leaving it to visible wear.

sections.html:
Built-Up Roof Systems on Winston-Salem's Older Commercial Stock

Built-up roofing, alternating plies of asphalt and felt or fiberglass reinforcement finished with gravel or a smooth cap, is less common as new construction today than it was decades ago, but it's still present on a meaningful share of Winston-Salem's older commercial buildings, and it's still a system we specify where heavy rooftop equipment loading or a specific fire rating calls for it.

Where Legacy BUR Shows Up in This Market

Some of the oldest commercial buildings downtown and around Winston-Salem's older manufacturing corridor still carry original or multiple-times-recovered built-up systems, often with a gravel surface that's been added to over the years without a clear record of ply count. Before we propose anything on a legacy BUR roof, we core it to establish exactly how many plies and recover layers are present, because North Carolina's building code limits how many layers can remain before tear-off becomes mandatory, and a gravel-surfaced roof can hide that history under the surface.

Asbestos-containing materials are a real possibility in roofing products installed before the 1980s, and we don't proceed with demolition on a legacy roof without appropriate testing and handling protocol where age and construction era warrant it.

Ply Count and Surfacing Options

New BUR installations typically run three or four plies, with surfacing options including gravel ballast, a smooth asphalt cap, or a mineral-surfaced cap sheet. Gravel ballast adds weight the deck needs to support but offers strong fire resistance and UV protection for the plies underneath; a smooth or mineral surface reduces dead load but requires more attention to maintaining surface integrity over time.

  • Existing ply count and layer history confirmed by core sample before any new work
  • Asbestos assessment performed on pre-1980s roofing material before demolition
  • Ply count and surfacing type specified against deck load capacity
  • Fire rating requirements confirmed for the building's occupancy classification
  • Drainage and slope assessed, since BUR is unforgiving of standing water at seams
  • Warranty tier confirmed against full assembly compliance

Deck Load and Structural Considerations

Gravel-ballasted BUR is among the heaviest common low-slope systems, and older decks weren't always designed with a future gravel recover layer in mind. We check structural capacity before adding weight to an existing deck, particularly on older manufacturing buildings where the original design load may not have anticipated the roof's current condition after multiple recover cycles over the decades.

Recover vs. Tear-Off on Legacy BUR

A BUR roof that's already at or near the code-permitted layer limit, or one where core samples show wet insulation under the surface, isn't a recover candidate regardless of how sound the surface looks. We document core findings and layer count in the proposal so the tear-off recommendation, when that's the outcome, is backed by data rather than a general age-based assumption.

Fire Classification and Insurance Documentation

Built-up roof assemblies carry their own tested fire classification, and on older buildings where original construction documents are incomplete or missing, an insurance underwriter or lender may request current documentation of the roof assembly's fire rating before renewing coverage or financing. We can document the installed assembly's specification against its tested fire classification for a new BUR system, which gives an owner a current record to provide when that request comes in rather than relying on decades-old paperwork that may not reflect the roof's actual current condition.

This becomes especially relevant on manufacturing buildings carrying legacy BUR roofs, where insurance requirements have tightened over the years in ways the original roof specification never anticipated.

Warranty Expectations on BUR Systems

Manufacturer warranties on new BUR installations follow the same tier structure as other systems, tied to ply count, surfacing type, and full assembly compliance. Because so much of our BUR work involves an aging building with an incomplete maintenance record, we also document existing condition thoroughly at the start of a project, which matters both for warranty registration and for any future ownership transfer.

Coordinating Tear-Off Timing With Building Operations

Legacy BUR removal on an occupied downtown or manufacturing building generates more dust and odor than single-ply tear-off typically does, particularly where gravel ballast has to be removed and hauled off before the underlying plies come up. We coordinate this phase with building management around HVAC intake locations and operating hours, since gravel removal and hot asphalt work, where torch or kettle methods are used on the new system, both carry operational considerations that a single-ply reroof doesn't raise in the same way.

Questions on Built-Up Roofing Projects

Is built-up roofing still installed on new projects?

Less often than single-ply systems, but it's still specified where heavy equipment loading, specific fire rating requirements, or an existing BUR maintenance history favor staying within the same system.

How do you know how many plies an old BUR roof has?

We core the roof in multiple spots to count plies and any recover layers added over the years, since a gravel surface can hide that history and code limits how many layers can remain before tear-off is required.

Could an older BUR roof contain asbestos?

It's a real possibility on roofing material installed before the 1980s, and we conduct appropriate assessment and handling protocol before any demolition on roofs from that era.

Does a gravel-ballasted BUR roof need a structural check?

Yes. Gravel ballast is heavy, and we confirm the deck can carry that load, particularly on older buildings that have already been recovered more than once.

What warranty applies to a new BUR installation?

Warranty tier depends on ply count, surfacing type, and full assembly compliance with the manufacturer's current specification, confirmed before the contract is signed.

items.name: Edge Metal, Coping & Gutters in Winston-Salem, NC
items.meta: Edge metal, parapet coping, and gutter installation and repair for Winston-Salem commercial roofs, fabricated and fastened to manufacturer wind uplift specification.

sections.html:
Edge Metal, Coping, and Gutter Systems for Winston-Salem Commercial Roofs

Edge metal and parapet coping take more wind load than almost any other roof component, and they're the detail most likely to be undersized or improperly fastened on buildings where roofing and general contracting scopes weren't well coordinated during original construction. We treat edge metal as a wind-uplift-rated assembly, not a finishing trim item, because that's the more accurate way to think about a component that's the first thing to fail in a high-wind event.

Wind Uplift Rating and Fastening Spec

Edge metal fastening patterns are governed by wind uplift calculations specific to the building's height, exposure category, and location, ANSI/SPRI ES-1 is the standard most manufacturers reference for edge securement testing. We calculate the required fastening spacing for the specific building rather than using a generic pattern, because a building in an exposed location off US-52 or along the I-40 corridor near Kernersville takes a different wind load than a similar building sheltered by surrounding structures downtown. Undersized fastening is one of the most common issues we find on older buildings during storm damage assessments, edge metal that was installed to a generic spec rather than the building's actual wind exposure.

Coping Systems on Parapet Walls

Parapet coping caps the top of a wall and sheds water away from the wall assembly and roof membrane below. A coping system that isn't properly lapped, sealed, and fastened lets water behind the parapet, which can saturate wall insulation and eventually find its way to the roof membrane from the inside of the parapet rather than the roof field, a failure mode that's easy to miss during a routine roof inspection because it doesn't originate on the roof surface itself. We fabricate coping to match the parapet dimensions on site rather than using stock lengths that require excessive field-cutting and additional seams, since fewer seams means fewer potential leak points.

  • Wind uplift calculation specific to building height and exposure category
  • Edge metal fastening spacing set to ANSI/SPRI ES-1 referenced specification
  • Coping fabricated to parapet dimensions to minimize field seams
  • Gutter sizing calculated against roof drainage area and regional rainfall rate
  • Downspout placement coordinated to avoid conflict with building entrances and loading areas
  • All metal work integrated with membrane termination per manufacturer detail

Gutter Systems and Drainage Capacity

Gutters on commercial buildings need to be sized for the actual drainage area they're serving and the regional rainfall intensity, rather than matched to whatever gutter size was there before. Undersized gutters overflow during the kind of sudden, heavy downpour common in summer thunderstorms here, sending water down the building face instead of through the downspout system, which over time can damage the wall assembly and undermine foundations at the base. We calculate gutter and downspout sizing against the specific roof area draining into that run rather than defaulting to a standard size.

Material Selection and Finish

Edge metal and coping are typically fabricated from prefinished steel or aluminum, with gauge and finish selected based on the building's exposure and the manufacturer's compatibility requirements for the membrane system it's terminating. We match metal specification to what the roof membrane manufacturer's detail calls for, since using an incompatible edge metal system can affect warranty coverage on the membrane itself, even though the metal itself isn't the membrane.

Repair vs. Full Replacement of Edge Systems

Not every edge metal issue requires full replacement. Where fastening has loosened but the metal itself is sound, we re-fasten to current wind uplift spec. Where metal has corroded, been dented in a storm, or was undersized from original installation, full replacement of that run is the more durable fix. We inspect the full perimeter before quoting, since a partial repair on one section while an adjacent section is equally at risk just defers the next failure by a short window.

Edge Metal on Buildings With Rooftop Solar or Added Equipment

Buildings that have added rooftop solar arrays, satellite equipment, or additional mechanical units after original construction sometimes have edge metal that was never re-evaluated for the added weight and wind exposure those additions create near the roof perimeter. We check edge and coping condition specifically at any zone near added rooftop equipment, since airflow disruption around new equipment can change wind loading patterns at the nearest edge or parapet section in ways the original design didn't account for.

Questions on Edge Metal and Gutter Work

Why does edge metal fail before the rest of the roof in a windstorm?

Edge and corner zones carry the highest wind uplift pressure on a low-slope roof, and if fastening spacing wasn't calculated for the building's actual exposure, that's typically the first place a wind event finds a weakness.

Can coping problems cause a leak that looks like it's coming from the roof field?

Yes. Water getting behind a poorly sealed parapet coping can travel down inside the wall assembly and reach the roof membrane from underneath the parapet, which can be mistaken for a membrane failure during a quick inspection.

How do you size a gutter system for a commercial roof?

We calculate based on the actual drainage area feeding that gutter run and regional rainfall intensity, rather than matching whatever size gutter was previously installed.

Does edge metal replacement affect my roof membrane warranty?

It can, if the replacement metal isn't compatible with the manufacturer's termination detail for the existing membrane. We match materials to the manufacturer's specification to avoid creating a warranty gap.

Do you repair sections of edge metal or only replace the full run?

Both, depending on condition. Loose but sound metal gets re-fastened to spec; corroded or storm-damaged sections get replaced, and we inspect the full perimeter first so we're not leaving an equally weak adjacent section untouched.
